title: Find a bad exporter entry when the service starts

blocks.text: The reporting service reads its exporters from a config file: `html=...HtmlExporter`, `md=...MarkdownExporter`, one class name per format. Two incidents last quarter: a misspelt class name went live on a Friday and was found by the Monday morning report, and an exporter nobody had used for months failed its own template setup and took the whole service down at startup.
`ExporterRegistry` already creates exporters from a working config. Finish the `TODO` in `src/main/java/practice/ExporterRegistry.java`:

items: `resolve(key, className)`: what the registry keeps for one config entry, worked out when the service starts.

blocks.text: When you're done, a config entry the registry can't use stops it from being built, with a `ConfigException` that names the entry's key, and building the registry runs none of the exporters' own setup: each exporter's class is set up when its first instance is created. About seven lines in total.
The tests use exporter classes nested in the test class, and pass you the class loader to use.

cases.says: each configured key creates a new instance of the class it names
a class name that doesn't exist fails when the registry is built, naming the key, not when that exporter is first created
a class that exists but isn't an Exporter fails when the registry is built, naming the key
building the registry doesn't initialise any exporter class; its static setup runs when the first instance is created

origin.section: Class.forName(name) Runs the Static Initialiser; the Three-Argument Form Waits for First Use

concepts: asSubclass checks a loaded class against the expected type at once; an unchecked cast of the Class object checks nothing and the failure comes where an instance is used.
Class.forName(name) runs the class's static initialiser; forName(name, false, loader) and a class literal load without it, and the initialiser runs at first instance or static access.
A class named in a string is looked up only when code asks for it, so a misspelt name fails at its first use unless startup resolves it.
